questions.q: Why is hardware and network failure considered routine, not exceptional, for a large-scale training run?
options: Because GPUs are inherently less reliable than other computer hardware
Because running on hundreds or thousands of GPUs for days or weeks multiplies the exposure to failure, even if each individual component's failure probability is low
Because training frameworks intentionally inject failures for testing
Because only cloud providers' hardware fails, not on-premises clusters
questions.explain: The sheer number of components in a large fleet running for an extended time multiplies the chance that some component fails before the run completes, even though no individual component is especially unreliable.

questions.q: What makes a silent hang harder to handle than a process crash?
options: Silent hangs are actually easier to detect than crashes
A crash is noticed immediately by the scheduler, but a hang -- such as a collective operation blocking on a degraded rank -- produces no error and no signal unless an explicit timeout is set
Silent hangs only occur on single-GPU jobs
Hangs always resolve themselves within a few seconds automatically
questions.explain: A crash is immediately visible to the job scheduler, but a silent hang -- like a stuck all-reduce waiting on an unresponsive rank -- produces no error at all without an explicit communication timeout, making the job appear frozen with no actionable signal.

questions.q: What does setting an explicit timeout on torch.distributed.init_process_group accomplish?
options: It prevents any GPU from ever failing
It converts a stuck collective communication operation into a raised error instead of an indefinite hang, making the failure detectable and actionable
It automatically increases the model's batch size
It disables all checkpointing during training
questions.explain: An explicit timeout ensures that a collective operation which would otherwise block forever instead raises an error, turning an invisible freeze into something the training stack can detect and react to.

questions.q: In the torchrun elastic launch example, what does --max-restarts=3 control?
options: The number of epochs the model will train for
The number of times the elastic agent will automatically restart failed workers before giving up, without the job being resubmitted by a human
The number of GPUs required per node
The learning rate warmup schedule
questions.explain: max-restarts bounds how many automatic restart attempts the elastic agent will make for failed workers before it stops trying, allowing recovery without manual job resubmission.

questions.q: Why are checkpoint cadence and fault tolerance described as one system rather than two independent concerns?
options: Because checkpointing has nothing to do with how a job recovers from failure
Because a restart is only as cheap as the most recent checkpoint it can resume from -- the fault-tolerance mechanism's effectiveness depends directly on checkpoint frequency
Because fault tolerance makes checkpointing completely unnecessary
Because checkpoints are only used for final model deployment, not for resuming training
questions.explain: When a restart happens, training resumes from the last checkpoint -- so how much progress is lost in a failure depends directly on how recently a checkpoint was saved, tying the two mechanisms together.
